1. Industrial Context and Problem Statement

This individual prototype addresses WP2 (Box Formation) in CEVA Logistics' proposed automation of value-added services, where box formation precedes kitting, sealing, packing and downstream handling. CEVA identifies manual box erection as an upstream bottleneck and calls for a system that releases erected boxes at a controlled rate, giving downstream equipment a predictable supply [1], [2]. A compact, low-cost mechanical former could reduce repetitive handling. This work covers the mechanical formation of tongue-insert cartons; line-pace control, operator interfaces and data integration remain wider WP2 functions.

2. Objectives, Scope and User Acceptance Requirements

The interim objective is to develop and evaluate a mechanism that positions a flat carton, erects its body, folds its side flaps, inserts the tongue and transfers the formed box to the output. Modular conveyor integration, recipe-based configuration and congestion-controlled release, also in the WP2 specification, are future integration requirements, not current capabilities.

The twelve WP2 user acceptance requirements (UATs) are listed in Table A1 (Appendix A). These are industrial targets, not prototype results. The prototype mainly addresses UAT-01 (4 s per box), UAT-02 (≥ 99.8 % success), UAT-05 (footprint ≤ 1000 × 1200 mm) and UAT-07 (no scratches); the rest concern utilities, controls and integration. The brief specifies tongue-insert and interlock boxes; this design covers the tongue-insert variant only, and suitability for the full box family remains to be verified.

3. Literature Review and Design Rationale

Automated carton forming typically separates blank handling, erection, flap folding and discharge into coordinated operations, each checkable for clearance, repeatability and carton damage. Options include guided mechanical folding, motor-driven arms and pneumatic pushers; suitability depends on carton geometry, force, cycle time, cost and changeover, and none suits every box type.

The CEVA–SIT proposal places WP2 within a sequence of kitting, packing and dispatch, and highlights high-mix, low-volume handling and faster SKU changeovers [1]. Based of the personally conducted research, none of the translatory models have been patented and major designs that are shown to function can be reverse engineered to make due within the speculated prototype.

4. Existing Market Solutions and Their Limitations

Three commercial machines were compared with manual erection (Table B1, Appendix B): the SM-YZT02 tuck-in carton machine [3], SiroSilo tuck-end box erector [4] and UBL high-speed carton folder [5]. Prices are indicative, not quoted.

Low-cost machines. Both leave unloading unsolved: the SM-YZT02 requires manual unloading and the SiroSilo erector a separate mechanism or an operator, so neither delivers a formed box onto a conveyor as WP2 requires [2]. The SM-YZT02 is also bought for one closure style, restricting changeover. The SiroSilo's rated 10,000 boxes per day is of the same order as the 7,200 boxes per 8 h in UAT-03, but its operating hours are not stated, and refilling its closed loading bay and conveyor linking need supplier confirmation.

High-end machine. The UBL folder's adjustable box settings and conveyor-linkable section match WP2's integration and changeover needs [2], but it handles only tongue-insert boxes, not the interlock boxes WP2 also specifies. At over USD 8,000 it costs 3.2 times the SiroSilo's upper price (USD 2,500) and 5.3 times the SM-YZT02 (USD 1,500).

Manual erection. It needs several operators, gives irregular boxes, and differing work speeds create the bottleneck that motivates WP2.

Implication. There is a gap between low-cost machines that stop at erecting and folding and a costly conveyor-linked machine limited to tongue-insert boxes. The proposed concept includes an output conveyor (Section 5) so formed boxes leave without manual unloading; whether it does so at lower cost and the UAT-01 rate is not yet shown, and no cost estimate exists.

5. Concept and Mechanical Arrangement

The concept combines a translating suction platform, passive spring-loaded erection struts and actively moved flap-folding elements (Figures 5.1 and 5.2). Four suction cups hold the flat blank on a rod-guided platform. The advancing carton pushes apart two triangular spring-supported struts beside the travel path, bringing its side walls upright. This passive erection needs fewer driven elements but is sensitive to spring preload, carton stiffness and geometry.

At the closure station, two L-shaped folders close the side flaps. A stationary upper housing guides a moving rectangular part whose trapezoidal tucker folds the major flap and inserts its tongue; an output conveyor receives the formed box. Separating the three operations lets each motion be checked independently.

Figure 5.1. SolidWorks isometric view of the assembly, with main components labelled.

Figure 5.2. Plan view of the lower layer: (1) suction platform with four vacuum cups; (2) spring-supported struts; (3) L-shaped side-flap folders; (4) fixed upper housing; (5) moving rectangular part with trapezoidal tucker; (6) platform guide rods; (7) output conveyor.

6. Working Principle and Preliminary Design Analysis

The intended sequence (Figure 6.1) is: (1) place a flat blank on the platform; (2) apply vacuum; (3) advance through the struts to erect the carton; (4) close the side flaps; (5) advance the upper element to fold the major flap and insert its tongue; (6) retract, release the box onto the conveyor and return the platform. The conveyor handoff is not yet defined.

Figure 6.1. Five-stage carton sequence (flat blank, erected body, side flaps folded, major flap folded, tongue inserted) and the element that produces each stage.

6.1 Carton Envelope and Loaded Geometry

The stated carton is 120 × 100 × 200 mm, giving an external bounding volume of

V=L×W×H=120×100×40mm3=4.8×105mm3V = L \times W \times H = 120 \times 100 \times 40\ {mm}^{3}\ = \ 4.8 \times 10^{5}\ {mm}^{3} (1)

(2.4 L external, not usable capacity). With the 200 mm side along the platform axis, the erected plan footprint is 100 × 200 = 2.0 × 104 mm². Figure 6.2 shows the assumed end geometry: a creased centre tuck flap and two short trapezoidal side flaps, hinged on an end fold line facing +y.

Figure 6.2. Loaded carton end as assumed in the animation (schematic sketch).

Taking one drawing unit as 1 mm (the 100 mm body is drawn 100 units wide), a 200 mm carton lying lengthwise would overhang the 168 mm belt by 32 mm (16 mm per side), so the animation draws it 170 units long. The carton's real orientation on the conveyor must be confirmed.

6.2 Erection Through the Spring Struts

The animation specified in the presentation idealises body width W = 100 mm, wing length a = 30 mm and strut gap g = 70 mm. With the wings raised through θ (0° flat, 90° erected), the projected carton width and each strut's displacement are

w(θ)=W+2acosθw(\theta) = W + 2a\cos\theta (2)
δ(θ)=w(θ)−g2\delta(\theta) = \frac{w(\theta) - g}{2} (3)

so δ falls from 45 mm (flat) to 15 mm (erected). Treating each strut as a linear spring of stiffness k, the force per strut is

F=kδF = k\delta (4)

An illustrative k = 0.2 N/mm gives 9 N per strut flat and 3 N erected, with compression falling from 75 % to 25 % of the 60 mm drawn spring (Table C1, Appendix C). The struts contact the 170 mm carton for about 186 mm of travel. None of these values is yet confirmed by measurement or CAD as the actual boxes are yet to be provided to us by CEVA as they maintain their boxes as controlled items.

6.3 Flap Folding and Suction Hold

A flap of length ℓ rotated through θ from flat projects a plan length

p(θ)=𝓁cosθp(\theta\mathcal{) = l}\cos\theta (5)

so the 30 mm wings project 30 mm flat, about 21 mm at 45° and zero upright. Folding torque for actuator selection follows from

T=Fr⊥T = Fr_{\bot} (6)

using measured flap resistance F and the actual perpendicular lever arm r⊥; no value is quoted as flap resistance is unmeasured. Suction capacity must exceed transport and erection resistance with margin. For n cups of effective area Ac at vacuum level Δp, friction coefficient μ and safety factor S, the requirement is

nμΔpAc≥SFresn\ \mu\ \Delta p\ A_{c} \geq SF_{res} (7)

where Fres combines strut drag and the carton's inertial load during platform acceleration.

6.4 Cycle Time and Drive Speeds

For a cycle time tc (s), the theoretical rate R (boxes/min) is

R=60tcR = \frac{60}{t_{c}} (8)

so tc = 4 s gives 15 boxes/min, consistent with UAT-03 (7,200 boxes / 480 min). The 28 s animation, as a sequential cycle, gives only 2.14 boxes/min and would need compressing sevenfold. Its timings are illustrative and cannot show that the machine meets or fails UAT-01. The mean and peak speed of each animated move (Table D1, Appendix D) follow from

v¯=dt,vpeak≈2v¯\overline{v} = \frac{d}{t},\ \ \ v_{peak} \approx 2\overline{v} (9)

with the peak about twice the mean for the smooth start–stop profile used. Retimed sevenfold, the 223 mm platform lift alone would need about 350 mm/s mean speed, so overlapped operations and faster drives must be examined; overlapping platform return with loading only shortens the sequence to about 25 s (2.4 boxes/min). A credible cycle time needs actual strokes, accelerations, overlaps and transfer delays.

These slowed observations are being made to understand and put into consideration the lack of knowledge of the exact stress limits of the boxes and the machine is slowed to a point slower than the resonance and any expected yielding stress the box or the machine may undergo.

7. Interim Progress, Design Risks and Evaluation Plan

The interim outputs are the SolidWorks assembly, an ordered process description and a two-dimensional animation of the intended motions. These communicate the concept but are not physical tests or force-based simulation. Open issues are the checks in Section 6.5 and the unverified spring displacement and force.

Verification should progress from CAD interference and travel checks to isolated trials: strut opening force and vacuum holding first, then repeated flap-folding and tongue-insertion trials recording closure outcome, cycle time, scratches and failure mode. Acceptance against the 99.8 % success rate and 7,200-box run is reserved for a mature integrated system.

8. Future Work and Interim Conclusion

Next steps are to confirm the box dielines; finalise spring, vacuum and actuator specifications while attempting to reduce the procurement cost of the raw parts for the next prototype; resolve guide travel and conveyor handoff; then fabricate and test the prototype. Control development must then address outlet-congestion stop/resume, recipe selection, throughput logging and ET1/RMF data exchange.

The interim design establishes a plausible staged mechanical approach to tongue-insert box formation, with a defined assembly and sequence that can now be tested against explicit acceptance requirements. Demonstrating production-rate operation, reliable closure and safe downstream integration remains future work.
